utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And this -- there are no protective measures sought for this witness, and it's Mrs. Slobodanka Hrvacanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort Mrs. Hrvacanin to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say as the witness is coming in, just to use the time, that there are occasions, I'm sure Your Honour will appreciate, where there are things which a witness, either on the Prosecution or the Defence side, is in some way bursting to tell the Court and will tell the Court anyway. It may not be rigorously, ruthlessly relevant. I just hope Your Honour will understand if sometimes for a relatively short passage such material is elicited in evidence even perhaps ruthless, rigorous efficiency about what was strictly relevant might exclude it. But, Your Honour, I'm talking about really quite minor things on which I could lead as quickly as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we'll hear from Mr. Tieger once leading becomes a problem for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Hrvacanin. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth. May I invite you to make that declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Hrvacanin. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. Stewart, who is counsel for the Defence. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Hrvacanin. Mrs. Hrvacanin, I'm going to put a number of facts to you fairly quickly to do with your own personal history and other basic matters. I'm going to invite you from time to time when I do that just to tell the Trial Chamber whether you agree or whether there are any corrections that you want to make. Now, you were born on the 31st of January, 1946 in Belgrade. You graduated from high school in Gradiska, which is about 58 kilometres from Banja Luka on the Sava River, and Croatia is just on the other side of the river. You gained a diploma in dentistry from university in Belgrade. Your father was a volunteer in the Serbian army in the First World War, fought on the Salonika front. He was a Thessalonika freedom fighter. In World War II he was for a time in the Stari Gradiska concentration camp. At one point he was taken out to be shot but narrowly escaped by virtue of somebody who recognised him being able to save him, and he was sent on the way to Germany. The convoy on the way to Germany was stopped in Zagreb and eventually he, with a number of others, made his way to Slovenia. Your mother was arrested in retaliation, sent to a camp in Germany, and because of your father's background as a freedom fighter his -- he found difficulty getting a job -- or you found difficulty as well at times. He found difficulty getting a job in what was then a communist state and went abroad at times to look for work. Now, is all that, as an important family background for you, Mrs. Hrvacanin, is all that I've just described accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were married in 1970, and when you were first married you lived and worked in Zenica, and you have one son who was born in 1972; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your husband, who is still alive, your husband was, during the communist era in former Yugoslavia a Communist party member, but you yourself were always and have always been strongly anti-communist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But in fact your husband's support of the Communist Party, which you always vigorously disagreed with, did at least help you to be able to finish your studies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you eventually gained a doctorate in Novi Sad, and you now work as the head of the dentistry department at the medical school in Banja Luka and as an oral surgeon in the health centre in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I'm an oral surgeon in Banja Luka in the health clinic, and I am dean of dentistry at the medical faculty in Banja Luka and a professor there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct that you have -- you have watched, from time to time, excerpts of this trial on television? On main television programmes there are from time to time summaries and reports of this trial of Mr. Krajisnik, and you have from time to time watched those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you at any time watched the internet transmissions of this trial?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, in Zenica municipality -- well, to just jump ahead for the moment: You stayed and lived in Zenica municipality, didn't you, until the end of February 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, in Zenica municipality in -- at the time of the multi-party elections in November 1990, what was the ethnic mix in Zenica municipality as you remember it? What proportions of the different nationalities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in -- most of it belonged -- 60 per cent was the Muslim population, 15 was the Croatian, and 50 per cent [as interpreted] the Serb population. The rest belonged to Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in the November 1990 elections --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there appears to be a transcript error that counsel may wish to correct with the witness in terms of the percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It appears in the transcript as 50 per cent Serbs. That may be just a mishearing. You said 60 per cent were Muslim, 15 per cent Croats, and then the percentage that you would put on Serbs is what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: The same as the Croats; 15 per cent. We were a national minority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then in the November 1990 elections, do you remember what the proportions of votes were that were obtained by the main parties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Most of the votes were won by the Party of Democratic Action, the SDP, and the Serbian Democratic Party and the HDZ got an equal number of votes. Then there was the party for Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav Party, the Green Party, and a few other minor parties. I don't know what percentage they secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I should have made it clear that my question related to Zenica. Your answer clearly did relate to Zenica. What was the -- can you put a percentage on the votes in the Zenica municipality that was obtained by the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: We won 10 per cent of the votes. Of the 15 per cent of the inhabitants we had, we had nine deputies in the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, did you attend a large meeting on the 12th of July, 1990, at the Bascarsija hall in Sarajevo which was a founding convention of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: About how many people do you remember being there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, there were 2 to 3.000 people there. It's a large hall. I don't know the exact number, but it was chock-a-block full. People were standing in the hallway as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Dr. Karadzic, Radovan Karadzic present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Izetbegovic present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the temperature of the meeting? Was it -- was it a good-natured meeting? Was it an argumentative meeting? What sort of a meeting was it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, it was a founding Assembly meeting. The atmosphere was very nice. The SDS was the third national party which was being established out of the SDA party and the HDZ party, and there was a general atmosphere of friendship that prevailed. There were no insults being hurled. All the speakers expressed their happiness that the Serbian Democratic Party was being founded. And when I say that, I'm not referring to people from the Serb ethnic group but from other ethnic groups who were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you previously been active in politics yourself before that meeting on the 12th of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: After that meeting, did you go to see Mr. -- Dr. Radovan Karadzic in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you go with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I went with people from Zenica. I went with Bosko Jevtic and some other people whose names I don't remember because, after all, it's been 15 years since then. We went to see how we were going to found the Serbian Democratic Party in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was Bosko Jevtic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Bosko Jevtic was a member of the initiative board for the founding of the Serbian Democratic Party in Zenica. He was a technician working in the ironworks of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he have some personal connection with you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I am the kuma, or godmother, to his children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there then a meeting in Zenica that followed your visit to Sarajevo to see Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: On that first occasion I didn't have chance to meet Dr. Karadzic, but did I have a chance of meeting his associates, and that was the late Danilo Veselinovic, Mr. Velibor Ostojic, Mr. Joja Tintor. Then we came on the second time and it was Mr. Radovan Karadzic. We had a talk and discussed how to form the Serbian Democratic Party in Zenica. He wasn't overjoyed with the idea, and he said that there were very few Serbs living in Central Bosnia. I don't know what he meant by "very few Serbs," or insignificant number if you know that there were 100.000 or maybe more Serbs living in that part of Bosnia, but then he said, "Well, all right. Do something, then," and we were given the basic instructions and guidelines as to how to establish the party. We joined up and started organising the whole affair, and in August the party was formed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there, please, Mrs. Hrvacanin. You said that you were given the basic instructions and guidelines as to how to establish the party. Could you give the Trial Chamber some idea of the nature of such instructions and guidelines.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, the party already had a statute. It couldn't have registered in the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina without the statute. So we had a statute, and from the statute we were able to see all the conditions met for the party to be established, that is to say what organs it should have. We expanded our initiative board of like-minded people, anti-communists who had spent their entire life during the communist era living under conditions of mistreatment and abuse, and we rallied around and tried to form this Serbian Democratic Party. And we had a solemn session similar to the one that was held in Sarajevo. There were many Serbs, a large number of Serbs, certainly over 800, perhaps more, in the hall, and the hall was a cinema that was called the 29th of November Cinema Hall in Zenica. It has a large hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, may I ask you to pause there. You -- you started off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just ask one brief question to clarify the matter. You mentioned the name of Joja Tintor. Is that the same person as Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, I was just going to say that you started off the first ten minutes or so with very short answers. Your answers are becoming a bit longer. If you could please tend towards the short side and then I will put more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes. Thank you, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No apology needed, Mrs. Hrvacanin. The -- were you given -- I've asked you about instructions and guidelines given. Were you given any policy directions on those visits to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Krajisnik on those visits to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you at the time know who Mr. Krajisnik was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Coming to the meeting that you were describing, then, that took place on the 28th of August, 1990. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic was present at that meeting, was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the president of the Zenica SDA also present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the president of the Zenica municipality, was he present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. Mr. Kolar is a Croat. Bogdan Kolar is his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you, on or shortly after that meeting on the 28th of August, take on the office of president of the SDS for the municipality of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: At that meeting I was elected president of the SDS of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that the first political post that you had ever held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any -- was there any unpleasant consequence for you personally of your becoming the SDS municipality president?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes, very unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: It was very unpleasant for me. After one of our meetings, the police collected me up off the street and took me to the premises which the State Security Service used. I thought that it was a friendly invitation as they told me when they took me over on the street to have a cup of coffee. However, later on it turned out to be something quite different. I was there verbally and physically abused. Perhaps the whole session would have lasted much longer had a good friend of mine not turned up, and he succeeded in extracting me from the clutches of the people who wanted to beat me. On that particular occasion I was just slapped twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That good friend of yours, was he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: He worked in the crime police. He was a crime inspector, but he did not work in the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you said that they took you over on the street to have cup of coffee. So they took you to the police station, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I was a doctor, and people would come to me from the police force as patients, and at first I just couldn't believe that anything bad would happen to me. That's what I always tend to think. I always tend to think the best of people, and I never have any fear that something bad will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many of -- were they policemen, all these people who took you to the police station?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: They worked for the State Security Service. They're not called policemen. They're inspectors of the DB, state security. They don't wear uniforms. They wear the kind of clothes that all of us ordinary civilians wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you got to the police station, was there a discussion or some form of conversation or questioning? What happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: First I had the cup of coffee that I was invited to. Then one of them told me to get up. I did get up. Then the cross-examination started: What is it that we Serbs wanted? Do we want to write in the Cyrillic alphabet? I said, "Well, the Cyrillic alphabet is our alphabet. What do you want?" "There's no place for you here. Go to Serbia and live there." I asked them whether that was some kind of a joke or whether they were serious when they said that. They said, "You don't even know what kind of situation you're in." I turned to one of them whom I knew, I didn't know the rest of them, and I said, "What are you doing?" At that moment I was slapped in the face. I was hit in the ribs too. He hit me with his elbow. And it was only then that I realised where I was. When I as a woman was being beaten, what happened to men?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any questioning or comment made on that occasion by these men on the policies of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: They said that all missions regarding the SDS had to be finished and that it would be best for me to leave the SDS if I wished myself and my family well. They said that they were vigilantly following everything that we Serbs were doing and they said that we were a national minority there; Muslims were majority. And one of the men who I already mentioned and who I said I knew from before, I think his last name was Vukovic, I cannot say whether he's a Serb or a Croat because I really don't know whether he is one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But he was one or the other and not a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I don't know what he was. But the remaining three men were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any suggestion made to you that any SDS policy on any issue should be abandoned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. Generally speaking, they were saying that the SDS had no business there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any reference made by anybody to Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I've already said that they abused me verbally. I am sorry, I do apologise to the Court, because I'm going to use a swear word. They cursed my Chetnik mother, and they said that we Chetniks had no business there. I don't think I'm a Chetnik. I'm a nationalist, a sound nationalist, no greater nationalist than a French person or a Dutch person or a Spanish person. I love my own people. I'm a Serb, and I shall always remain one, but I respect all other peoples, all other nations, all other religions, because as a Christian I cannot live any other kind of life. I did not think that I was there to answer questions as a Serb, but I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any mention by anybody in that discussion of the idea of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: That was said often. A Greater Serbia was often mentioned. I think that we just wanted to be equal to the other two peoples, the Muslims and the Croats, and the other peoples living there. In Zenica there are over 30 different ethnic groups. There are Czechs, Germans and others who came to the town where the steelworks were being built. So I don't see why anybody would have that kind of idea in that area. We wanted to live in Yugoslavia, and we wanted to be within Bosnia-Herzegovina, our state, at that time a republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you mention to these men that you had personally any support for the idea of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. Why would I support the idea of a Greater Serbia when I lived in that town, when I lived in that republic? I was born in Belgrade. My mother is a Belgrader too. But I was born towards the end of the Second World War. My father suffered terribly in the Second World War and he didn't want to go on living in Gradiska where he was born because, as a Serb, he was mistreated by the communist regime. He wanted us, his children, and I'm the ninth child of my father, to have a safe and happy future. However, I'm sorry that I have to say this, I'm 60 years old but I'm not happy today either. Can a person like me be happy, who was expelled from the town of Zenica on account of the fact that she's a Serb, whose property was not restituted? My husband cannot get his pension, and I cannot be happy for as long as such issues are at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, we -- the incident that you've just described took place, we know, between your election as the SDS Zenica president and the multi-party elections in November 1990, so just concentrating on that period for the moment, from the end of August until the multi-party elections in November 1990, did you experience any other unpleasant consequences of your -- or what you understood as consequences of your election as SDS president in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: This is the Balkans. It is very hard for a woman in the Balkans to be a public figure and to be involved in cultural affairs. Women, like in the Ottoman Empire, are supposed to stay at home, take care of their families and husbands, their children. This was a great burden for me because I was mistreated every day. I had these telephone calls at work, at my workplace. They cursed my Chetnik mother. They were saying that I should move out. They threatened me over the telephone. They threatened to kill me. When I walked through town until then I was a well-respected figure through my profession, but then I had thousands of embarrassing situations. They would mock me and shout "SDS, you will wear a fez." That's what they shouted after me. In many places, in the marketplace where I went shopping for my family, they would call out my name from several different directions in order to frighten me so that I'd leave the marketplace. When I'd get home, the telephone would ring and the question would be, "Are you still there? Move out. We're going to kill you. We're going to kill your son. We're going to kill your husband. You've got to leave." And this went on for months. Often in my mailbox I would find threats, threatening letters. They tried to explain to me that my name was ugly and that my last name was nice, because Hrvacanin probably made them think of Croats; Hrvat. They said, "It would be best for you to get out of here." Under the door I would find little notes saying, "There's a grenade in your apartment. We're going to kill you. What are you waiting for? Why are you not leaving?" All of that led to my decision in February 1992 that I leave the town that I lived in, that I leave it forever. I lived in that town. I never made a mistake there. I looked at all of my patients as patients. Ethnicity or religion or race did not matter at all. I was what I was because, after all, I took the oath of Hippocrates and all people are equal to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, you -- you've described a number of types of incident, and you referred very often to "they." "They would call out my name. They would mock me." Who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did incidents of this type that you've just described over the last few minutes begin before the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I put a question? I don't understand. Are you referring to the parliamentary multi-party elections or the party elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mrs. Hrvacanin. I was referring to the November 1990 multi-party elections throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina for the, among other things, the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly. So I'm talking about -- the time I'm talking about, I think it was the 24th or 25th, the time I'm talking about is the end of November 1990, and the question was whether incidents, those telephone calls and those sorts of incidents, did they start before those elections?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Before the parliamentary elections, yes. Not before the party elections. While the party was being founded, it seemed that the SDA and the HDZ wanted to topple communism first and foremost and that that is what would happen, that the communists would no longer be in power and that non-communists would get into power.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there, in that period before the parliamentary multi-party elections, were there any actions or was there any behaviour in your locality on the part of Croats that you found objectionable?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. As for Croats, there was an increasingly visible coalition between the Muslims and the Croats. Their pre-election rallies were terrifying. They had flags there, and of course it didn't really suit any Serb to see that. They were very vociferous at these rallies, so all of this instilled anxiety among the Serb population of Central Bosnia, especially when the SDA had their Congress in the Holiday Inn hotel. I think it went on for three days. At this Congress Mr. Brozovic, who is a Croat from Croatia, was a guest, and he said that the eternal dream of the Croats to establish a border on the Drina River would finally come true. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene for a better understanding of your testimony. You were talking about Croats, that they had flags and that it didn't really suit any Serb to see that. You continued, "They were very vociferous at these rallies, so all of this instilled anxiety among the Serb population of Central Bosnia, especially when the SDA had their Congress in the Holiday Inn hotel." You switched from the Croats to the Muslims, and then immediately continued with Mr. Brozovic who was, as a Croat, a guest. Did you mean to say the SDA Congress or were you referring to the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Mr. Brozovic attended the SDA Congress. That was the SDA Congress, not the HDZ Congress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Brozovic was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You referred to flags. The transcript may not have it a hundred per cent at the moment, but in some way actions and in relation to flags were not acceptable to Serbs. What was it that you were talking about there, what actions connected with flags?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: For example, the SDA flag and the Croat flag, the chessboard flag, were tied together. And then there were Saudi Arabian flags at these rallies too in Velika Kladusa. There was a lot of kind of this folklore, so to speak, which does not belong to our country, which was then called Yugoslavia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Serbs did no such thing. They were not tying up flags that way. We came to rallies, too, but without flags and without baiting others. In the local media, the television, radio, and the daily press, there were many statements to the effect that Muslims were the flowers of Croatdom. I as an intellectual did not mind not being anybody's flower, but the messages I was receiving were that I would not fare very well. I came to that conclusion myself without anybody even telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does the phrase -- what did the phrase "The flower of Croatdom" or "The flower of Croats," did that have any resonance for you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I'll try to explain that. As a woman, I am very fond of flowers. I like giving flowers as a present. I like having flowers in my home, I like having flowers in my garden. People who do not like flowers and who do not know what it's like to take care of flowers do not know what beauty is. When you pay that kind of compliment to someone, then it means that that person means the world to you. Knowing history, knowing what happened in the Second World War, and having been fortunate enough to live with a father who spent the First World War and the Second World War the way he did, I didn't like that because I realised that there was something going on and that this coalition would probably do something bad, which later proved to be true in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just pause there for a moment. The phrase "The flower of the -- of Croatdom," did it have any specifically political or historical resonance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. The Croats and the Muslims were allies in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any phrase used in the Second World War in any way related to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I was born after the Second World War. I was born in 1946. But I know that Muslims were part of Ustasha units and that they cooperated closely with the Croats. You yourself said that my father was from Gradiska, and the concentration camp of Stara Gradiska was right there and all the people of Gradiska know that history.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, leaving the incident you described at the -- when you were taken to the police station or the state security station, but did you take any action yourself as a result of that incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Sarajevo to say that to Mr. Karadzic and to the political council of the party that held its meetings in Sarajevo on Mondays. I was worried for myself, and I was worried about other people who were top intellectuals. I was worried that something could happen to them. Mr. Karadzic did not consult me but made this public at a press conference. I think that it was held on the second day, on Tuesday. Of course, the state security of the SUP of Zenica responded by saying that they had not brought me into custody and had not beaten me. They don't have any written record. However, I must say that communists never had any written records for people they brought into police custody and beat up. No police records are required for that. But I had a record on my face, on my eye, and in my soul, and I still feel this trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there, before the parliamentary elections in late November 1990, an incident affecting your apartment in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, can you -- can you date that incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you when that happened. I think it was the 8th of August. I have a document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you mean August?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm just not sure now. I've become a little upset telling the story I've been telling. But on the document it says -- I can show you the document if His Honour the Judge will permit me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mrs. Hrvacanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have the document and over the break we will arrange necessary copies. I can proceed without the document, but, Your Honour, I can tell you it relates to 8th of November, 1990. It's very clear on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it in your hands, Mr. Stewart, whether it's -- and also I don't know whether this is a contested matter, yes or no. If not, then even without the document we could accept the testimony of the witness as such. We should take care that -- we should take care that -- I do understand that this is much of background information on what happened elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the same time, it goes into such detail that now and then the question came into my mind whether you were presenting the Prosecution's case in a case to be started against Croats and Muslims rather than whether you are presenting the Defence case, in view of the charges against Mr. Krajisnik. So therefore the level of detail and the balance, I leave it up to you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can do, for example, in relation to -- to this incident, I could more ruthlessly lead on the matter, Your Honour, and get to it quite quickly, and then if Mr. Tieger, or indeed Your Honours, had any problems with what I was leading, then of course you could say so at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we will. I hope that you got the other part of my message.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, and I know that my job is to defend Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And charges against him rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed Your Honour, I'm well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I shall follow that as my guiding principle, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- is this right, Mrs. Hrvacanin, that on the 8th of November one of the nurses where you work recognised a man who was inquiring about your whereabouts as a Ministry of Interior employee and that later that day your son told you on the telephone that your apartment had been broken into and ransacked, with things strewn about, and that had in fact happened? When you got home, you discovered that there was a terrible mess of your apartment, with belongings and clothing strewn about, that very little was stolen, just a little bit of foreign currency. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you did report the incident to the police straight away; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And inspectors came to the apartment, took fingerprints, were there for several hours, but after that you never received any further response to your complaint?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: That's right. The inspectors did come and so did the investigating judge. They made a note of it all and kept a record of it. They didn't give me an answer, nor did they when I filed a criminal report against the police of the Zenica district.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- in -- around April of 1991, is it correct that you were elected to a further SDS position which was the president of the region of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if I can just torment the interpreters for a moment, if I read off - and everybody else - a list of municipalities, can you confirm that these are the municipalities which comprised that region: Zenica itself, Kupres, Bugojno, Donji Vakuf, Travnik, Vitez, Zavidovici, Zepce, Magla, Kakanj, Busovaca, and is it Novi Travnik/Pucarevo? Were those all comprised in the region of which you were elected SDS president?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that's 12 municipalities. Is it correct that, at least in theory, Gornji Vakuf was also included but there were no Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: A small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Zenica had, is this right, for some considerable time been effectively the centre of that particular region?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Zenica was the centre of the region according to the state set-up as well. Not only the one that the SDS had but previously as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On your appointment, or election, rather, as the president of the Zenica municipality - and I'm talking about the municipality now - did you become a member of the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. In the first mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that was your first mandate, and then, just jumping ahead for the moment in time, then, when did your second mandate begin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: In 1991, on the 12th. St. Peter's Day, the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- under whichever mandate, did you remain a member of the Main Board of the SDS right through from the end of August 1990 until late into at least 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: The term of office was four years; until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you -- until well after the end of 1992 you were continuously a member of the SDS Main Board after your initial membership. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In Zenica itself after the multi-party elections, were you involved in leading for the SDS in power-sharing discussions at the municipality level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they were tripartite discussions, were they; the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And for the SDS there was you as the SDS president and nine local deputies who were Serbs, is that right, in the negotiations, power-sharing discussions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. Each party gave a certain number of negotiators; the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS. So that we were engaged in certain agreements that you would think were fine at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who led for the SDA in those discussions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: At the head of the SDA delegation was the president of the municipality, Ibrahim Alispahic, who was elected president of the municipality. Well, maybe I've got the surname wrong. I apologise if I do, but I know that his first name was Ibrahim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And for the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: He was the number one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And for the HDZ, was it a Mr. Zakic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your part.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Sakic. That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And those negotiations took about three months altogether, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But one way or another you were able - is this correct - to obtain for the SDS rather more -- a rather higher percentage of the posts than was strictly proportionate to your votes in the election?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you obtain for the SDS around 30 per cent of the posts available?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the secret of your success in obtaining that higher percentage? How did it -- how did you achieve that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I negotiated with Mr. Ibrahim. Probably my patience and his patience was great. He wanted to help. He wasn't one of the extremist extremes of the SDA, and that was shown later on, and he was replaced as the president of the municipality and another man put in his place, because in fact he had given us more space than he ought to have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is this right, if I put a number of positions to you, that you were able to obtain for the Serbs, for the SDS, the following posts: Vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, vice-president of the Municipal Executive Committee, the headship of four of the 12 municipal departments, the position of secretary for public transport within the police, and also that there were no significant changes among directorships and managerial -- senior managerial positions in local companies? Is that description and list accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Everything that you have said is correct except for the SUP. Not the head of transport but the head of the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the chief of police and chief of state security, under the power-sharing arrangements, were both Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it right that at no time did you form a Serb Assembly in either Zenica municipality or in the central region of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you involved yourself in any power-sharing discussions in any other municipalities apart from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Only in Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And why did -- why were you involved in those discussions in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: The president of the SDS of Zepce asked me because only five and a half or 6 per cent Serbs lived there. It's a municipality with an equal number of Muslim inhabitants and Croat inhabitants, and he wanted me to become involved in that respect and I did. I tried to hold consultations and help in that way with respect to the power sharing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you become aware, in April and May 1991, of any imminent changes in relation to JNA presence in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. The garrison from Zenica was supposed to move out, and that led to another reason for nervousness and fear among the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Taking it just in stages, Mrs. Hrvacanin. Did you find out that -- in advance that the -- the men in the JNA garrison in Zenica were going to be moved to Cacak in central Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, you found out from one of your patients?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: That's right. The pilots who from Pleso, Croatia, came as logistics to the SUP of Zenica, I think there were three or four pilots. One was a patient of mine. I operated on him. He said this since they used the hangars for the helicopters and they were helicopters with which -- or, rather, which were supposed to be placed at the disposal of the medical centre because the Zeljezara mine was there and if there were any emergencies and natural disasters, they were to be deployed, and then he said to me, "Do you know that they're going to -- the army is going to pull out of here?" And I was astounded. I said, "No. That is the first time I hear of it."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, again I'm going to put to you a brief summary and ask if you can confirm it: That you learnt that the JNA from Zenica were going to move to Cacak. You went with a number of your Zenica SDS colleagues to raise this concern with one of your colleagues, a Mr. Ostojic. Not Velibor Ostojic, a local Mr. Ostojic who was in the nature of the local minister of defence under the power-sharing arrangements. Is that right so far?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: That is right. His name is Branko Ostojic, and he was the chief of the department for the army. I don't know what the exact name was, I didn't do any military service, of course. It was the National Defence Department, or sector. I think that's what its name was. But we went to see him and asked him whether that was true. And he was a lawyer by profession, he was a civilian, but he worked --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, I'm going to put the next bit to you and see if you agree with this. He did look into the matter. He told you that on the JNA pulling out of Slovenia, that a garrison from Ljubljana would move to Zenica, and that did happen about two months later, under the command of a colonel who later became a general, Tomislav Sipcic. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: That is correct, but the army didn't pull out. It was forced out of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- did the arrival of the JNA from Slovenia, did that have any effect on the feelings of the local Serb community in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. With the arrival of the JNA, the Serbs once again breathed a sigh of relief because they thought that everything would be all right, because our defender was there, our saviour was there, and everything would be well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As you came to -- to observe it as best you could, were you yourself satisfied and happy about the number of JNA soldiers who arrived in Zenica from Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: As they had no logistics, that is to say they didn't have doctors, dentists, I was called to the garrison to offer medical assistance to some of the officers and people working there in need of medical care. What I saw made me very frightened. Nothing was properly in order. Nothing was in its proper place. It was all untidy, and it appeared to me as if that garrison was going to move away in the near future, and that instilled fear and unrest in me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you visit the garrison in Zenica after Colonel Sipcic had arrived on Army Day, 22nd of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. The more prominent people from political life and from the authorities always for the 22nd of December, Army Day, were invited to attend a traditional luncheon of beans in the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, there was -- it doesn't matter whether there still is, but there was at that time, wasn't there, a substantial steel mill in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: There was a steel mill in Zenica, yes, and there was the Simmons Martin Steelworks as well. Ironworks and steelworks. I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did the steelworks have its own territorial -- have its own arms? Weapons I'm --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: The steelworks had its territorial arms because -- territorial weapons because they stretched over a piece of land which was 15 kilometres. It's an enormous area. They had their own security system, and they had 17 entrance gates for their employees. It was a giant, employing 23.000 workers. It's heavy metallurgy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you learn at any time in late 1991 or early 1992 of any acquisition of arms by the Zenica steel mill?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I -- it is the ironworks of Zenica, or the term being used is steel mill. Well, in 1991, we had no salaries or, rather, not regular salaries. And when we did receive something, we would receive coupons which would allow us to buy food and items of personal hygiene and household goods. I asked one of the directors of the internal bank, Mr. Martin Janjevic, "When are we going to receive our salaries?" and he said, "We have a lot of expenditure at the present. The ironworks had ordered automatic rifles and when we pay for those automatic rifles, that's when you'll receive your salaries." I wondered what we would need automatic rifles for. I wasn't a man. I wasn't a soldier. And that was rather strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When did you first learn about this order of automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Secondhand. I heard that things like that were being bandied about town, and I heard it for the first time from this gentleman, that it would be procured and paid for. And the media published that afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mrs. Hrvacanin, I was asking you when you first learned about that order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. I think it was the beginning -- or, rather, the end of the summer and beginning of the autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the middle of 1991, in the summertime, around June or July 1991, did you notice any -- anything unusual or any change among the people that you saw in your part of the city; Jalija, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, I saw people cleaning, who were engaged in cleaning the town, keeping it clean. And I saw in my neighbourhood six or seven people there, which wasn't normal, because there was either one or none at all to cater to that part of the town, just the garbagemen following the garbage truck. And they were located there. And when I passed by I would usually say, "Hello. Good morning. How are you?" That's what my parents taught me to say. And I saw, judging by the way they spoke, that they didn't speak our language very well. And then I became interested in finding out who these people were, and I was told that they were people who had come in from Kosovo and who the new utilities director had employed to keep the town clean and that there were a number of them. Later on, my knowledge was gained from people who, when I'd left Zenica -- that is to say I learnt secondhand from others that these were the cadres of the green -- future Green Berets, and the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had -- had any men arrived at any point in 1991 that you were aware of from Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: From Sandzak I don't know about that. I'm not aware of that. In Sarajevo there were a number of people from Sandzak. Since I was doing my oral surgery specialisation course there in Sarajevo and I saw that there were lots of people from Sandzak coming in. But there was something else that I noticed, actually, and it was this: In the drugstore where I make my purchases, which is close to my flat, I saw foreigners buying there, and they were paying in dollars. I had previously said that we ourselves were not receiving salaries. It was an Upi market store and we had coupons for that particular store and that's how I was able to buy my goods. I asked the woman working at the cashier's who these people were, and she said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I just interrupt you? You referred to foreigners. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, I think they were Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said you asked the woman who these -- the cashier -- the cashier in the supermarket who these people were, and then I interrupted you with that question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. The cashier said that they were foreign students, because Zenica at that time had technical faculties, such as the faculty of metallurgy, the faculty of electrical engineering, the faculty of law, and so on, and that they had come in as students to study there. I found that a little strange, because it was the end of November, beginning of December. I was a student myself, and I know that studies usually begin in October, not in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did you -- were you able subsequently to find out whether they were students or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what did you discover?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: My patient was Professor Sulejman Drljevic from the faculty. It was a faculty within the frameworks of our ironworks at Zenica, and I asked him what foreign students they had received just now, and he said, "We haven't got any foreign students, Mrs. Hrvacanin, or not as far as I know." And I asked him, "Are you aware of the fact that in town people like that -- there are people like that in town?" And he said, "Well, I did hear something about that." And although he was a Muslim, he was a cosmopolitan, he was a man who didn't mind what religion you were or what ethnic group you belonged to, just like me, and he said, "Perhaps they're Mujahedin," and that was the first time I heard of the word Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, as president of the Zenica SDS, hold a regular press conference at this time every Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you raise this matter at a press conference?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I declared that and made that public at a press conference and said that foreigners had arrived in Zenica, Mujahedin, because rumours were already going round that a Patriotic League had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: After you raised the matter at the press conference, did you become aware of any change connected with these foreigners that you had identified as Arabs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, after a certain amount of time they disappeared from our area. Perhaps I and a few other Serbs lived in that neighbourhood which was otherwise an exclusively Muslim neighbourhood, so that they were dislocated and moved to a neighbouring village which is called Sarici, near Nemila, and that is a place which is about 15 kilometres away from Zenica and the village is 30 kilometres away from Zenica, up in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock. I wonder if that would be a convenient point for Your Honours to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a convenient time for a break. We will have a break until five minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm handing to the witness what's -- a document that's been seen before in this court. May I ask for it to go onto the ELMO. It's very familiar, Your Honour. It's the item that's numbered 93. We'd chosen that as the particular example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May it be put on the ELMO. My guess would not being wrong if I was thinking about the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour would be really getting in the right region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, are you able to see a document? I don't know whether it would be more convenient for another copy to be available.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I can see the document but only --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just -- if you need --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- to see the actual document at any point, Mrs. Hrvacanin, as opposed to seeing it on the screen, please don't hesitate to say. Now, Mrs. Hrvacanin, had you ever seen this document or a document like it before you arrived in The Hague in the last few days?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you, before you arrived in The Hague -- and you arrived in The Hague last Thursday night, didn't you? You arrived Thursday evening in The Hague. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of a document known as Variants A and B?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you in Sarajevo at any time in late December 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say -- and I'm talking about the second half of December 1991 now. Are you able to say on what dates you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I think it was the 19th, 20th, and the 21st when I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And for what purpose were you in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I think that the Assembly was in session that day, the Serb Assembly. I wanted to attend that Assembly in the Assembly building. I think that some important items were on the agenda. I found them important; what the coat of arms would be and what the anthem would be in the republic -- or, rather, this was on the agenda of the Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, can we just get a couple of things clear, Mrs. Hrvacanin. You were not at any time a deputy in the Serb Assembly, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On that -- that visit to Sarajevo, did you attend any meeting of the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: You mean the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the visit that you've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: It wasn't only the Main Board. This was a bigger meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, if we can try and stick as specifically as possible to my questions. On that visit to Sarajevo, did you attend a meeting of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I don't know about the Main Board having a meeting on the 19th. I was at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was open, was it, to you, although not a deputy in the Serb Assembly, to attend Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: That's right. Mr. Krajisnik, who was president of the Assembly, allowed people who wished to attend to attend; people from politics, ministers, representatives of municipalities that did not have their own MPs. He allowed them to attend the Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say "allowed," was it a -- in the nature of a courtesy that Mr. Krajisnik should give permission or was there any question of anybody being refused attendance at the Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Krajisnik is a democrat, and he never refused anyone. At least, I'm not aware of him not allowing someone to attend Assembly meetings. He never refused my requests, but I've never heard of him refusing anybody's requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So were there at that Assembly meeting -- was there quite a number of people present who were not actually deputies in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, first of all, in what building did the Assembly meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: The session took place in the so-called Blue Hall of the municipality building. It was the Assembly of the B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said the -- the Blue Hall of the municipality building. Is that a correct description of the building, the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Assembly building, yes, Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did that meeting take place in the morning or the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: From around 10.00 onwards. Until lunch, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the meeting ceased or broke for lunch, did it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At a normal sort of time, around the middle of the day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the meeting subsequently resume in the Blue Hall on that same day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you leave the Assembly building for lunch?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: The Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you personally went to the Holiday Inn. Was that a general move? Did all or a large number of the people at the meeting in the Blue Hall go over to the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- I was waiting, but this is clearly an area where I would ask counsel to refrain from leading questions to the extent possible. A couple of the previous questions have gone in that direction, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd rather have the non-leading questions in this portion of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. I'm obviously being asked to be ultra-strict, and I will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you -- did you -- did you arrive at the Holiday Inn and have lunch there yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you lunch alone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. Everybody had lunch there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did anybody who had -- as far as you knew, did anybody who had been at the meeting in the blue room remain in the Assembly building when you went over for lunch to the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any -- any sort of meeting that you were involved in at the Holiday Inn before you had lunch?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: It was an expanded meeting. The members of the Main Board were there, members of parliament were there, then some ministers were there, and the representatives of some municipalities that did not have MPs of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, may I just be -- be specific about this. I asked you about before lunch. The expanded meeting, leaving aside for the moment any details of that meeting, but the expanded meeting that you referred to, that began before lunch, did it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was before lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did it conclude before lunch?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Perhaps two hours, perhaps less. I could not say exactly, but it wasn't long.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How far is it from the Assembly building to the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I don't know the exact distance, but I can tell you how much time it takes to get there: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Five minutes by what? What means of movement or transport?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: By foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you walk over?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember anything particularly about the day in question when you walked over from one building to the other?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, I saw some people in the street wearing green berets, and I asked some people, "What is this? Is this some new kind of police in Sarajevo?" And nobody knew how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about the day itself, what sort of a day it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: It was pretty cold. It was windy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you described the meeting as an expanded meeting, where exactly did it take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: The meeting took place in the Congress hall of the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What sort of size room is that? Is it -- is it bigger than this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: A bit. Just a little bit bigger. Perhaps it's just a bit longer, and narrower on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know whether we need to record the measurements of this courtroom, Your Honour. We're in the very large courtroom III this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it -- was the expanded meeting a -- whoever was there, was it officially a meeting of some specific organ of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. It was a spontaneous meeting, because there were things going on and the deputies had a discussion. I think that this was the time when the platform on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being prepared. I think that at the same time Mr. Silajdzic attended some Congress of Islamic countries where he presented certain views that caused concern among the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many people were at the expanded meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I think over 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And could you -- you gave some -- some description of who were there. You said members of the Main Board, members of parliament, ministers, representatives of some municipalities. Any other categories of person who were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps drivers of some ministers and technical staff that was there to provide their services if necessary, if somebody needed a telephone or whatever. There was no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In what capacity did you regard yourself as attending that expanded meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, I was there as a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able to say how many municipality presidents were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: A few, a small number. These were municipalities that did not have MPs of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How -- how familiar were you with the municipality presidents for the SDS throughout Bosnia? That's to say did you -- what proportion of them did you know personally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I knew some well and others I knew only by sight and with some I was actually friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you -- would you be able to say whether there was any particular category of municipality which was better represented at the meeting than others?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. No one was represented in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who presided over that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: The president, Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you remember who else of the senior figures in the SDS were present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Velibor Ostojic was present, Mr. Rajko Dukic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik was present, too, but he was not chairing the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From -- can you describe where Dr. Karadzic stood and what sort of furniture he was working with when he presided over the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was sitting there. It was like the Honourable Judges are sitting today. So that was the group of people who were chairing the meeting. And opposite them were the members of the Main Board, the Executive Board, the MPs, and the other guests on chairs, and there was a rostrum on the other side where the lady tells us that the session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Karadzic -- did he have other senior figures of the SDS seated close to him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I've mentioned it was Mr. Dukic, and Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they sat with him at some sort of table, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: They were chairing the meeting. They were sitting at the chairman's table.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik sitting at the chairman's table?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. He sat where the rest of us sat, in the first row.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Miroslav Deronjic at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Just by sight as a member of the Main Board from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was he at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Radomir Neskovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. He's a founder of the Serb Democratic Party. He was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- did you know Mr. Neskovic more or less well than you knew Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mr. Neskovic better. As a matter of fact, he was a guest in my house. When he needed something, I was always there to help him; money, cigarettes, spending the night, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct you still have a personal relationship with Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Yes. He lives in Banja Luka. We see each other. We talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does he still come to your home at times?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No. We see each other at a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was -- can you remember what was the topic, if there was one, of discussion at that expanded meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I've said that the entire political situation was very heated. I know that Muslims were making certain decisions, and after that it was inevitable for the Serb MPs to leave the Assembly. They left the Assembly, and they formed an Assembly of their own. It was this declaration that was being discussed. People were worried. By the very recognition of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would the Serbs be in a position to be out-voted all the time, and what would the position of the Serb population be in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you -- do you know of any other similar size meeting that took place in the Holiday Inn in December 1991 relating to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it possible that such a meeting was held without your having known about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: I think that that would not be possible. Knowing myself, I think that they could not hide something like that from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Broadly speaking, Mrs. Hrvacanin, what sort of contacts and relations did you have in December 1991 with active SDS members around Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Well, at that time the SDS Assembly was being prepared. Sorry, were you asking about 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking specifically about December 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN
utterances.text: Specifically I did not have any particular duties. It's not that I had to do something for the SDS somewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, there are, for example, people who just keep themselves to themselves. They get on with their job, they come to the meeting, they go home, they don't talk to anybody, they don't socialise. There are people like that. Are you that sort of person?
